title: Nonequilibrium Transient Centers in Continuous-Time Systems
abstract: Analysis of mathematical models in ecology and epidemiology often emphasizes asymptotic dynamics, such as stable equilibria, periodic orbits, and attractors. However, many biologically relevant trajectories exhibit long transient dynamics in which a relevant observable evolves slowly for an extended period before a comparatively rapid transition occurs. On finite time scales relevant to data collection, management, and intervention, such transient behavior can be more informative than the eventual asymptotic outcome. In this work, we study long-lasting and slowly varying transient dynamics in continuous-time systems through the framework of nonequilibrium transient centers. These centers are points in the state space near which the observable can remain nearly constant for a long time, even when the full state is not near an equilibrium. We develop finite-time escape criteria for identifying such centers and their reachable counterparts. These criteria provide practical conditions under which nearby trajectories can remain in a slow regime for a long period of time before eventually leaving it. We apply the theory to an epidemic model with delay of stability loss. In this model, trajectories may remain close to the disease-free manifold for a long time before the infectious population resurges. The framework developed here describes this behavior as slow evolution near a nonequilibrium transient center followed by finite-time escape from the slow regime.

title: ChatGPT as a Surveillance Assistant? An Exploratory Case Study of AI-Assisted Surveillance Risks
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate detailed guidance, functional code, and persuasive text at scale. As one of the most widely used consumer language model products as of 2026, ChatGPT gives broad public access to these capabilities, motivating concerns about its potential use in surveillance-related tasks. We present an exploratory case study of what potentially harmful surveillance assistance looks like in ChatGPT's public web interface. We contribute a taxonomy of seven surveillance risk categories based on prior LLM risk research and reports of deployed surveillance systems, instantiated as 110 prompts, along with a manually reviewed analysis of ChatGPT's responses. Prompts were issued using two approaches: 55 jailbreak prompts drawing on five types of elicitation strategies, and 55 plain-language direct prompts, each run alone, and if unsuccessful, again with a short fixed prefix. We find that ChatGPT provides substantive surveillance guidance for 40 of the 55 jailbreak prompts and for 33 of the 55 direct prompts without any prefix. Compliant responses also rarely included policy mentions or suggestions for privacy-preserving alternatives. We manually review every response and find that even when ChatGPT states a refusal, it may still supply detailed instructions, working code, or architectural guidance alongside brief ethical caveats.

title: Mosquito acoustic identification at unseen recording sites: practical limits of common transfer remedies for vector surveillance
abstract: Passive acoustic monitoring could widen mosquito surveillance, but a classifier trained under one set of recording conditions often fails when moved to a new site, device or enclosure. On a nine-species, five-condition corpus of about 271,000 recordings, the published baseline identifies species at 0.881 balanced accuracy under conditions it has seen and 0.175 under held-out ones. Using that corpus's leave-domain protocol, we asked which transfer strategy is most reliable when a program brings a new site online. Using fixed features from a pre-trained bioacoustic model and a small classifier improved held-out-condition balanced accuracy to 0.305, without updating backbone weights and in minutes of training per site. Four widely used additions did not improve transfer: rebalancing training across recording conditions, fine-tuning the backbone and fusing a weaker second modality each reduced accuracy, and a six-term objective reduced to a single alignment term. Rebalancing reversed direction across four encoders, helping weak representations and harming strong ones. Genus-level aggregation was more accurate than species-level classification (about 0.50 against 0.30), suggesting genus-level screening may be the more realistic operating point here. These results come from one corpus under one protocol, and are dataset-bounded guidance rather than validated general rules.

title: Who Gets Watched? Allocating Scarce Escalation Resources on Pediatric Wards with Neural Index Policies
abstract: Problem definition: Hospitals use separate pathways to identify and respond to deteriorating ward patients. At Children's Healthcare of Atlanta (CHOA), these include Watcher surveillance, Critical Care Outreach Team assessment, and transfer to the intensive care unit. When several patients need attention simultaneously, however, no common process determines who should receive which response under limited staffing and capacity. We study how to coordinate these actions to support earlier escalation without unnecessary monitoring. Methodology/results: We model ward escalation decisions using a multi-action restless multi-armed bandit model and develop Multi-action Index Learning and Optimization Policy (MILOP) as a computational solution approach. MILOP trains a neural network to generate a high-quality index policy using a decision-focused learning approach. We train and evaluate MILOP using historical CHOA data and compare it with two practical baselines. MILOP recommends an escalation before 87.4% of critical or emergent intensive-care transfers, compared with 79.5% for the stronger baseline, while using 13.5% less monitoring resources. MILOP provides a median of 19.2 hours lead time before transfer, earlier than either baseline. Moreover, 99.3% of MILOP's proactive transfer recommendations are preceded by Watcher surveillance or outreach-team assessment, demonstrating a desirable escalation of care. Managerial implications: MILOP can help leaders focus scarce clinical attention, gain more time to respond before severe deterioration, and reduce monitoring burden compared to existing practices. Broadly, hospitals may improve escalation decisions by coordinating existing pathways rather than managing each separately or using risk scores as stand-alone decision rules.

title: A stochastic epidemic model with memory of the last infection and waning immunity
abstract: We adapt the article of Forien, Pang, Pardoux and Zotsa, on epidemic models with varying infectivity and waning immunity, to incorporate the memory of the last infection. To this end, we introduce a parametric approach and consider a piecewise deterministic Markov process modeling both the evolution of the parameter, also called the trait, and the age of infection of individuals over time. At each new infection, a new trait is randomly chosen for the infected individual according to a Markov kernel, and their age is reset to zero. In the large population limit, we derive a partial differential equation (PDE) that describes the density of traits and ages. The main goal is to study the conditions under which endemic equilibria exist for the deterministic PDE model and to establish an endemicity threshold that depends on the model parameters. The local stability of these equilibria is also analyzed. The endemicity threshold is computed for several examples, including models that incorporate a vaccination policy, and a local stability result is obtained for a memory-free SIS-type model.

title: Mapping urban heat from citizen-collected data: a scalable Gaussian process approach to correcting for preferential sampling
abstract: The urban heat island (UHI) effect amplifies heat stress in cities, increasing heat-related illness, mortality, sleep disruption, and energy demand. Because UHI intensity varies at neighborhood scales, intra-city temperature mapping is essential for assessing public health impacts, yet existing monitoring networks are sparse. Crowdsourced weather stations provide dense, hourly observations but suffer from noise and systematic biases, including preferential sampling driven by where residents install sensors. We introduce two scalable Gaussian process frameworks which adjust for preferential sampling and enable statewide, high-resolution temperature prediction. The first integrates sampling correction directly within a sparse variational Gaussian process (SVGPR+PS). The second uses a two-stage estimator involving a log-Gaussian Cox process (LGCP+GP) that estimates the sampling intensity field and incorporates it into temperature prediction. Both methods rely on inducing-point approximations and variational inference to scale beyond traditional Gaussian processes. Applied to approximately 10,000 citizen stations across North Carolina, the models generate hourly temperature fields within minutes. Validation against independent urban heat campaign data shows that the preferential sampling correction improves predictive performance, increasing average afternoon correlations across four cities from 0.26 to 0.43. This scalable framework enables neighborhood-level UHI assessment and supports studies of heat exposure disparities statewide.

title: Kierston & KierstonBench: Simulation of Allentown, PA and Evaluation of Language Models in Crime Investigation and Surveillance Tasks
abstract: Large language models are candidates for collecting and analyzing records in criminal investigations and mass surveillance. Their capability and accuracy in this work cannot currently be measured. Real deployments lack the ground truth needed to score a model's conclusions, and no benchmark evaluates these capabilities in a simulated environment. We present Kierston, a city-scale simulation engine, and KierstonBench, a benchmark that tests these capabilities against known simulated events. Kierston models approximately 125,000 residents of Allentown, Pennsylvania, generating their daily activities and the telecommunications, financial, administrative and license-plate records that surveillance and investigative systems collect about them. These records derive from a common behavioral timeline and are distributed across sources representing separate providers. Models investigate through a restricted records interface, linking observations across sources without access to the underlying simulation. The benchmark comprises 32 task families covering record linkage, routine reconstruction, incident investigation and assessment of deceptive accounts. In an evaluation of sixteen language models, most could not perform records investigation and submitted identifications the records did not support. A small number of frontier models solved most of the tasks and abstained when evidence was insufficient. In some cases these models still fell for common deceptions and assumptions, and none replaced an investigator.

title: Same Question, Different Answers: Auditing Persona-Dependent Variation in Six LLMs on Smoking-Cessation Advice
abstract: Hundreds of millions of people now ask large language model (LLM) chatbots for health advice, which raises a question that is simple to pose and hard to answer: does everyone get the same advice? We audit six widely deployed LLMs from four providers on smoking cessation, a domain with codified clini- cal guidance and substantial public-health stakes, by putting the same four cessation questions to twelve user personas that differ in life stage, self-described expertise, and smoking history, for a total of 2,880 responses. What the models say depends on who appears to be asking. Every model named FDA-approved prescription cessation medications less often to teen personas than to adult personas, by 32 to 67 percentage points, and in five of six models a persona presenting health- care expertise received fewer facts than a persona presenting none. We then evaluate one deployable intervention: a short system prompt specifying a factual floor, the set of core med- ical facts every user should receive when they are relevant, while leaving tone, vocabulary, and framing free to adapt. The prompt narrows persona differences in every model, but its effect on overall fact coverage varies in both magnitude and direction across models, so a prompt validated on one system cannot be assumed to transfer to another. Two cautions frame these results. Equal mention rates are not always the correct clinical target, because prescription cessation pharmacother- apy is not recommended for minors, so a defensible factual floor must be age-aware rather than uniform. And because our personas vary on several attributes at once, we report scenario- level differences rather than isolated effects of age or expertise. We release all 2,880 responses and the analysis code.

title: Traffic-VL: Reinforced Vision-Language Models for Generalizable End-to-End Traffic Signal Control
abstract: Existing traffic signal control methods typically rely on structured traffic states produced by dedicated perception pipelines. Emerging visual approaches often use idealized simulator images and convert them into intermediate representations before control, limiting their ability to directly exploit roadside visual observations. To bridge both the visual-domain and perception-to-decision gaps, we introduce SynTra-V and Traffic-VL. SynTra-V converts physics-based traffic simulations into photorealistic multi-view surveillance imagery across diverse road topologies and sensing conditions, and automatic semantic auditing checks that control-critical geometry, vehicle movements, and lane semantics match the simulator state. Traffic-VL is an eight-billion-parameter vision-language model that directly maps synchronized multi-view images and natural-language phase descriptions to signal decisions without intermediate structured states. Building on Traffic-R1's two-stage reinforced reasoning framework, Traffic-VL adapts its vision encoder via offline reinforcement learning on SynTra-V and freezes it during online visual stepwise trajectory policy optimization in closed-loop simulation. Experiments show that Traffic-VL matches structured-state Traffic-R1 while outperforming image-based controllers and general-purpose vision-language models, including Gemini 3 Pro. Evaluations on unseen topologies, degraded sensing conditions, real surveillance footage, and a three-week deployment across ten intersections further demonstrate robust visual generalization and effective constrained online control.

title: Deep-Learning Algorithm for Indeterminate Thyroid Nodules: Comparison and Combination with Molecular Testing
abstract: Thyroid nodules with indeterminate cytology (Bethesda III) carry an intermediate risk of malignancy, and molecular testing is widely used to decide between surgery and surveillance, but it is costly and not universally available. We investigated whether a convolutional neural network (CNN) applied to routine ultrasound images can stratify Bethesda III nodules, and how it compares and combines with molecular testing. We retrospectively identified 466 nodule records from 418 patients who underwent molecular testing (Afirma or ThyroSeq). A CNN pre-trained on determinate nodules was adapted to indeterminate nodules with soft labels and transfer learning. After removal of duplicate records, 119 nodules with surgical pathology were used for development and 47 were held out for testing. On the test set, the deep learning (DL) model achieved an AUC of 0.73 (95% CI 0.51-0.94), compared with 0.55 (0.38-0.71) for molecular testing (P = 0.15). At a cut-off inherited from the original algorithm, the DL model was more specific than molecular testing (0.95 vs 0.32; P < 0.001), with a higher positive predictive value (0.67 vs 0.21), a lower sensitivity (0.44 vs 0.78; P = 0.25) and a similar negative predictive value (0.88 vs 0.86). All six DL-positive test nodules were molecular-positive, and the DL output split the molecular-positive nodules into a high-risk (4/6 malignant) and a lower-risk group (3/27 malignant; P = 0.01). Surgical verification was strongly driven by the molecular result (99% of positive vs 19% of negative results), and molecular-test accuracy depended on the platform. A logistic regression of the DL output, nodule size and the molecular result dropped the DL term and did not improve on the DL output alone. Ultrasound DL complemented molecular testing for Bethesda III nodules, in particular by identifying molecular-positive nodules at lower risk of malignancy.

title: Modeling and analysis of a novel two-strain dengue epidemics model considering secondary infections with increased mortality
abstract: In this study, we develop and analyze a deterministic two-strain host-vector model for dengue transmission that incorporates key immuno-epidemiological mechanisms, including temporary cross-immunity, antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), disease-induced mortality during secondary infections, and explicit vector co-infection. The human population is divided into compartments for primary and secondary infections, while the mosquito population includes single- and co-infected classes. ADE is modeled through distinct primary ($α$) and secondary ($σ$) transmission rates. Using the next-generation matrix method, we derive the basic reproduction number $R_0$ and establish the local stability of the disease-free equilibrium for $R_0 < 1$. Analytical results show that one-strain endemic equilibria lose stability under ADE conditions ($σ> α$), allowing invasion by a heterologous strain. Employing center-manifold theory and numerical continuation (COCO), we demonstrate the occurrence of backward bifurcation, bistability between disease-free and endemic states, and Hopf-induced oscillations. Numerical simulations confirm transitions among disease-free, endemic, and periodic regimes as key parameters vary. The model highlights how ADE, waning cross-immunity, and vector co-infection interact to generate complex dengue dynamics and provides insights useful for designing effective control and vaccination strategies in dengue-endemic regions.

title: Rethinking Optimization Methods for Hierarchical Feature Selection
abstract: Rare-event forecasting often depends on interpretable conjunctions: a single keyword, location, or temporal cue may be weak, while their joint occurrence can identify a meaningful precursor. Hierarchical-Task Numerical conjunctive feature Learning (HTNL) selects Numerical Conjunctive Features (NCFs) through a structured sparsity objective. However, the resulting optimization problem is challenging, making optimization design critical to its practical performance. We give a unified diagnosis of four HTNL optimization families: original majorization-minimization (MM), variational quadratic form (VQF), alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), and weighted group lasso (WGL). Our analysis distinguishes three key factors that jointly determine HTNL optimization behavior. First, VQF and MM are algebraically equivalent under matched variational updates and optimize a squared-penalty formulation. Second, ADMM optimizes the unsquared objective through consensus splitting; we replace its truncated FISTA proximal solver with a scalar bisection update (ADMM-Bisect) for more accurate treatment of near-threshold blocks. Third, WGL targets the same unsquared objective, while all methods face rapidly decaying active-set admission scores. Across two synthetic datasets and 11 civil-unrest and flu-surveillance tasks, VQF achieves the highest mean AUC with the most compact non-collapsing supports. ADMM-Bisect reduces measured runtime, while calibrated WGL avoids the empty-support failures of its original scale. Synthetic results further show how proximal accuracy, pruning, and search budget affect candidate recovery, especially for longer conjunctions. Code will be made publicly available upon publication.

title: Universal Infectious Disease Forecasting with Mantis 2
abstract: Public health agencies need to anticipate how outbreaks will unfold, when they will peak, and how long demand on health services will remain elevated. We previously developed a foundation model, Mantis, which was trained entirely on simulated outbreaks---enabling us to generate the diversity and scale of training data needed to support forecasting across diseases. However, our previous work left unresolved when simulation improves predictions and how it should complement observational data. Here, we varied the balance of simulated and observed training data while holding forecasting tasks fixed and varying the available surveillance history. We found that simulation-rich training was particularly valuable with limited local history, and its relative advantage diminished as more observations became available. We also found that simulation-based training reduced exceptionally large forecast errors, suggesting that mechanistic knowledge can help compensate for limited local evidence. Building on these findings, we developed Mantis 2, which combines simulated and observational training to jointly forecast up to six variables sixteen weeks ahead. Across 30 forecasting tasks, Mantis 2 achieved the best aggregate probabilistic accuracy over short, medium, and long horizons among the machine learning, statistical, and baseline models evaluated. It missed roughly 30\% fewer outbreak peaks than the strongest comparison model, with successfully anticipated peaks identified more than six weeks in advance on average. We publicly release Mantis 2, enabling public health agencies and researchers to forecast disease outcomes without developing a separate model for each disease or location.

title: Food Critic: An Agentic Visualization System for Auditable Restaurant-Safety Reasoning
abstract: Generative AI agents are increasingly being embedded into visualization systems that can search data, invoke tools, summarize evidence, and produce recommendations. However, when agents rely solely on their own knowledge, the visualization problem is not only whether the agent provides a useful answer, but also whether users can inspect how that answer is grounded. We present Food Critic, an agentic visualization system for diners' restaurant decision support that integrates public health inspection records with crowd review data. The system grounds agents under three conditions: a database-only ReAct agent, a retrieval- augmented agent with access to food-safety regulations, and an ontology-guided agent that produces structured hypotheses and typed evidence. Food Critic externalizes the agent's reasoning within these groundings as inspectable visual evidence. We evaluate LLM models with several use cases under each grounding of our agentic system. Our work positions restaurant choice as a concrete case for studying human-agent collaboration, visual provenance of agent reasoning, and the design of visual interfaces for grounded GenAI decision support.

title: Federated Learning for Cross-Regional Epidemic Forecasting with Asynchronous Outbreaks
abstract: Objective: Epidemic outbreaks are often asynchronous across regions, yet collaborative forecasting is hampered by privacy laws and heterogeneous public health interventions. We developed and evaluated, as a proof of concept, a federated learning (FL) framework for cross-regional COVID-19 forecasting under asynchronous outbreaks among Guangdong, Macau, and Portugal, while maintaining data sovereignty. Methods: Using daily case data from WHO and China CDC for the three regions, whose outbreaks were asynchronous and interventions heterogeneous, we trained Long Short-Term Memory networks via FL for short-term forecasting, benchmarked against localized and centralized training using Root Mean Square Error, Mean Absolute Error, and Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error. All experiments used the Flower FL framework with consistent hyperparameters across sites. Publicly available, aggregated case-count data were used so that the centralized benchmark could be computed as a reference. Results: The dataset comprised 1,233 daily observations (411 days) of new confirmed COVID-19 cases from November 24, 2021, to January 8, 2023. The earlier Omicron wave in Portugal supplied transmission dynamics that improved forecasts in the later-onset regions of Macau and Guangdong. The FL model achieved a normalized Root Mean Square Error of 0.028, an 88.3% improvement over the local model (0.240) and comparable to the centralized model, with network overhead mainly determined by model size and aggregation rounds. Conclusion: FL achieved short-term forecasting accuracy close to centralized training while maintaining data residency, with acceptable overhead. Leveraging asynchronous outbreaks across regions may offer a practical path to privacy-preserving collaborative forecasting, though prospective validation is required.

title: Towards Scalable Network-Based Interventions for HIV Treatment and Prevention via R2C-Agent
abstract: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) remains a pressing public health challenge worldwide. Targeting limited HIV prevention and treatment resources effectively with network-based algorithms is a long-standing problem with a rich history at AAMAS and other computational venues. However, optimizing targeted biomedical interventions for minimizing spread of HIV often requires observability of the contact network of HIV transmission risk behavior among individuals, which is prohibitively expensive to collect at scale. Peer referral networks, i.e., networks collected through a recursive peer referral process, are an alternative network class often used to study HIV in hidden populations that can be collected digitally at scale, but they deviate from the underlying contact network: referrals can follow non-risk social ties and participants accept only one referral, hiding contacts among already-recruited individuals. In this work, we first formalize the novel problem of planning network-based interventions to minimize HIV spread in the hidden contact network while observing only the peer referral network. Second, we implement R2C-Agent, a decision making agent for interventions that is designed around our new conditional graph diffusion model called Referral-to-Contact Diffusion (R2C-Diff). R2C-Diff positions the peer referral process as incremental corruption of the underlying contact network and learns to reverse it. R2C-Agent plans its interventions over contact networks sampled from R2C-Diff, so its decisions account for uncertainty about the hidden contact network. Finally, we conduct simulated experiments using real-world HIV network data that demonstrate that R2C-Agent empirically plans more effective interventions than baselines from interdisciplinary literature and highlight key tradeoffs and assumptions driving performance.

title: A Computational Map of the Disaster Mental Health Research Landscape
abstract: When disasters strike, they not only damage infrastructure, buildings, and the economy, but also affect the mental health of affected populations. Research on the mental health effects of disasters has expanded rapidly and has become an important, well-funded area of psychology, public health, and related social sciences. However, the overall structure of this research landscape has not been systematically characterized. Using large language models, we conducted a review of all articles related to terms 'disaster' and 'mental health' indexed in PubMed. 7,859 articles' metadata were retrieved using the NCBI API, and then Claude Sonnet was used to extract structured variables from the abstracts. The results indicated that earthquakes and epidemics were the most commonly studied disasters while many other disasters such as heat and cold waves have received less attention. PTSD, depression, and anxiety were well investigated but many other mental health issues (e.g., aggression, suicide) are relatively ignored. Despite enjoying relatively large sample sizes (median = 452, IQR = 142 - 1,568), the field rarely utilizes machine learning algorithms. Hypothesis significance testing, reviews, qualitative methods, and structural equation modeling are respectively most common methods while agent-based modeling, machine learning, casual inference, and NLP each appear in less than 1% of articles. Studies are limited to a small number of countries, particularly the United States, Japan, and China, while many disaster-prone regions remain substantially underrepresented. This LLM-assisted computational map provides a broad overview of the disaster mental health literature while highlighting important methodological gaps, with particular emphasis on the underutilization of computational methods that could help advance the field.

text_all: A Computational Map of the Disaster Mental Health Research Landscape When disasters strike, they not only damage infrastructure, buildings, and the economy, but also affect the mental health of affected populations. Research on the mental health effects of disasters has expanded rapidly and has become an important, well-funded area of psychology, public health, and related social sciences. However, the overall structure of this research landscape has not been systematically characterized. Using large language models, we conducted a review of all articles related to terms 'disaster' and 'mental health' indexed in PubMed. 7,859 articles' metadata were retrieved using the NCBI API, and then Claude Sonnet was used to extract structured variables from the abstracts. The results indicated that earthquakes and epidemics were the most commonly studied disasters while many other disasters such as heat and cold waves have received less attention. PTSD, depression, and anxiety were well investigated but many other mental health issues (e.g., aggression, suicide) are relatively ignored. Despite enjoying relatively large sample sizes (median = 452, IQR = 142 - 1,568), the field rarely utilizes machine learning algorithms. Hypothesis significance testing, reviews, qualitative methods, and structural equation modeling are respectively most common methods while agent-based modeling, machine learning, casual inference, and NLP each appear in less than 1% of articles. Studies are limited to a small number of countries, particularly the United States, Japan, and China, while many disaster-prone regions remain substantially underrepresented. This LLM-assisted computational map provides a broad overview of the disaster mental health literature while highlighting important methodological gaps, with particular emphasis on the underutilization of computational methods that could help advance the field. title: Key Institutional Considerations for Designing Effective Independent Verification Organizations
abstract: Independent verification organizations (IVOs) have emerged as a popular, bipartisan solution for facilitating high-quality independent evaluations of AI technologies. But momentum is outpacing design: there is emerging consensus on the necessary operating conditions for robust IVOs, but little discourse on institutional and policy specifications to ensure those conditions are met. IVOs are currently envisioned primarily as a mechanism operating at the AI frontier and model level to evaluate catastrophic risks. Little work has yet been done on how to establish or enforce an IVO ecosystem that is equipped to handle myriad risks (i.e., beyond catastrophic ones) and operate at the system and application level across the deployment and use stages of the AI lifecycle. This paper argues that IVO design should ensure the capacity for evaluating AI models, systems, and applications in context for both frontier companies and enterprise companies & AI-adopting organizations. Additionally, this paper provides early considerations to advance IVO discourse from normative to operative, and from existential to everyday risks. Drawing from existing institutional constructs in financial services, education, public health, and science, we outline key considerations on whom IVOs serve, what access they require, how they interact with external governing structures, how they are funded, and how they fit into the wider assurance ecosystem. Much of the structure and knowledge necessary to holistically design IVOs and their ecosystem does not yet exist, even as companies rush to ink agreements with their chosen evaluators.

title: Fine-Grained Generative Hallucination Detection and Correction for Aerial Image Captioning
abstract: Aerial imagery captured by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) plays a vital role in applications such as surveillance, disaster response, and large-scale environmental monitoring. Automatic generation of textual descriptions for such imagery is essential for reducing manual inspection overhead and enabling better downstream decision-making. However, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), despite their impressive captioning capabilities, are prone to hallucination, producing descriptions that are inconsistent with the visual input. This problem is significantly amplified in aerial imagery due to its unique challenges such as extreme viewpoint variation, small objects, class imbalance, and ambiguous visual entities. Existing hallucination detection approaches either rely on computationally expensive large external models such as GPT-4, which perform poorly on aerial domains, or treat the problem as a rigid binary classification task, ignoring the inherent uncertainty in ambiguous cases. To address these limitations, we propose a lightweight, reference-free framework for hallucination detection and correction in free-form aerial image captioning. Our method leverages state-of-the-art MLLMs, specifically InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL, to detect hallucinated content in generated captions with minimal computational overhead. Detected hallucinations are corrected through a dedicated refinement module that improves the factual consistency of the original captions. Extensive experiments on the Labelled Illusion Dataset (LID) demonstrate that our framework significantly reduces hallucination rates while remaining practical for real-time deployment in resource-constrained environments. Code is available at: https://github.com/Debolena7/Hal_Detect.

title: Bayesian inverse problems and epidemic-threshold uncertainty for a heterogeneous SIS reaction-diffusion model
abstract: We study Bayesian inference of persistence from early observations of a heterogeneous susceptible--infected--susceptible (SIS) reaction--diffusion model with standard incidence. We show that the leading prevalence dynamics depend on the unknown coefficients only through the difference between the transmission and recovery rates and the infected diffusivity. The same pair determines the principal eigenvalue whose sign governs persistence, so early prevalence can inform the threshold even when the individual rates remain uncertain. We prove global weak well-posedness and quantitative parameter stability for the SIS system and use the resulting observation-map estimates to establish Bayesian well-posedness. For an initial infection of size $\varepsilon$, we derive a uniform second-order expansion that describes how the separate rates enter prevalence. Incidence depends explicitly on transmission at leading order. When the noise standard deviation is proportional to $\varepsilon$, we prove $O(\varepsilon)$ convergence in Hellinger distance of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits for both prevalence alone and joint prevalence and incidence data. We bound the principal eigenvalue using the growth rate of the infected $L^2$ norm between two times. This rate gives a lower bound for the full nonlinear system, and the upper bound separates spatial transients from nonlinear saturation. Uniform spectral estimates and bounds on infection size and measurement error give sufficient conditions for persistence and extinction. We also bound the error in posterior persistence probabilities under forward and eigenvalue approximation, accounting for posterior mass near the threshold. Numerical examples illustrate threshold inference and the predicted \(O(\varepsilon)\) convergence of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits in Hellinger distance.

title: Benchmarking large language models for parameter-level structural identifiability classification in epidemic ODE models
abstract: Structural identifiability determines whether unknown parameters can be uniquely recovered from ideal model outputs, making it a prerequisite for interpreting parameter estimates. We evaluated whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably provide preliminary structural identifiability classifications for epidemic models. We constructed a retrospective benchmark of 88 scenarios from 14 of the 27 studies considered, encompassing 696 parameter-level formal reference classifications from published results or Julia-based symbolic analysis. Scenarios were evaluated using Domain-Aware and canonically relabeled ("Domain-Anonymized") prompts, with ten runs per configuration and prompt condition. Six configurations completed all scheduled responses, yielding 83,520 parameter-level decisions for the primary comparison. GPT-5.5 Instant and GPT-5.5 Thinking Medium had the highest accuracies among complete configurations (88.71% and 88.07%). Canonical relabeling improved both configurations and attenuated their performance decline in scenarios with many unknown parameters or state variables, although effects differed across model families. Locally identifiable parameters were the most difficult class (highest strict recall among complete configurations: 42.00%), although the local reference set was small. In multivariable analysis, each additional unknown parameter reduced the odds of correct classification (OR 0.881; 95% CI 0.852-0.910), whereas additional observed outputs increased them (OR 1.666; 95% CI 1.503-1.846). Exploratory evaluations indicated strong performance for GPT-5.5 Thinking High and Claude Opus 5, despite incomplete coverage. LLMs may generate preliminary hypotheses or flag cases for formal review, provided outputs are checked against published results or formal symbolic methods. They should not be used to certify the structural identifiability of a complete model.

title: Fractional-Order Hybrid SIR Forecasting of COVID-19 in Bangladesh and the United States: Memory Effects and Out-of-Sample Evaluation
abstract: Fractional-order epidemic models are often justified by memory, yet whether memory improves forecasts is rarely tested out of sample. We extend a hybrid SIR framework, in which a daily transmission rate is reconstructed from reported cases and then forecast, to Caputo fractional order $α\in(0,1]$. We prove well-posedness, conservation, positivity and a linearized threshold at disease-free states, and derive a Grünwald-Letnikov reconstruction that reduces exactly to the integer-order one at $α=1$. Our main theoretical result shows that for $α<1$ the influence of the unknown initial infectious count vanishes, but no faster than $t^{-α}$; after 332 daily steps it is about $4.4\times10^{8}$ times larger at $α=0.9$ than at $α=1$. In out-of-sample forecasting over 27 weekly origins, the effect of memory depends on the setting. In Bangladesh the integer order gives the lowest error for linear and constant-rate forecasts in 47 of 48 settings. In the United States, where reported cases reached about 18% of the population, a fractional order lowers the linear forecaster's error in all 12 comparisons in 2021 but raises the constant-rate forecaster's, with no difference significant after Holm adjustment. Against standard baselines, the SIR-based linear forecaster was more accurate than the classical SIR model and a neural network without SIR structure, and competitive with ARIMA: in the United States the fractional linear forecaster had the lowest error of all methods (seven-day MAPE 7.54% against 9.14% for ARIMA), whereas in Bangladesh ARIMA had the lowest MAPE, with no significant difference from ARIMA in either country. The choice of a fractional order should rest on out-of-sample evidence rather than in-sample fit.

title: A Markovian SuASR epidemic framework with stochastic external factors
abstract: Epidemic waves are often shaped by uncertain external drivers, such as environmental variability or behavioral and policy changes, that can randomly amplify or dampen transmission. Capturing this randomness requires models whose dynamics evolve under time-varying, stochastic influences. In this paper, we introduce a stochastic Susceptible-Asymptomatic-Symptomatic-Removed (SuASR) framework that embeds random external factors directly into the epidemic mechanism through an extended continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC). The proposed framework is flexible enough to represent epidemic dynamics both with reinfection and with infection-induced immunity, depending on the epidemiological setting under study. Unlike standard Markovian epidemic models, our formulation explicitly tracks two concurrent infectious sources (asymptomatic and symptomatic), yielding coupled infection pathways and substantially richer transient behavior. A key contribution is analytical tractability, where we derive computable expressions for the joint distribution of asymptomatic and symptomatic infection-event counts and develop tools tailored to extreme-outbreak risk, including the distribution of the maximum infectious burden. These results enable probabilistic quantification of epidemic severity beyond mean trajectories, providing direct estimates of the likelihood of rare but consequential surges. We validate the model through extensive sensitivity analysis and an application to the H1N1 influenza epidemic, illustrating how stochastic external influences reshape outbreak profiles, total infections from both sources, and the probability of extreme epidemic scenarios

title: Modeling Drug Overdose Mortality Levels Using Social Vulnerability Indicators in U.S. Counties: A Double Machine Learning Approach for Causal Analysis
abstract: Drug poisoning mortality (DPM) remains a leading cause of death among working-age Americans, and its burden falls unevenly across communities. Existing county-level studies of social vulnerability and overdose have largely reported predictive or associational relationships, while the shape of the adjusted exposure-response relationship between overall social vulnerability and mortality remains unclear. We examined the CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and county drug poisoning mortality across three two-year windows spanning 2016-2021. The associational analysis compared linear regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost models of log mortality using period-specific SVI subfeatures and county covariates. The selected XGBoost models were interpreted with SHAP values. The double machine learning (DML) analysis estimated the exposure-response relationship between SVI and DPM and tested the linearity restriction. Socioeconomic vulnerability contributed positively to predicted mortality, with disability and unemployment among the strongest subfeatures, while racial and ethnic minority composition contributed negatively in all three periods. Summing the four theme contributions reduced the overall-index attribution by 34% to 36%, indicating substantial offsetting. Linearity was rejected in every window ($p < 10^{-26}$). The adjusted relationship increased through the middle of the SVI distribution and declined in the upper tail. This pattern remained stable both before and after the outbreak of the epidemic. Overall SVI therefore captured meaningful variation in overdose mortality but did not function as a uniformly increasing risk scale across its full range. Component-level interpretation and current overdose surveillance provide important context for interpreting the composite index.

title: Global stability and uniform persistence in an epidemic model with saturating fomite-mediated transmission
abstract: We analyse the global dynamics of a Susceptible--Vaccinated--Exposed--Infected--Recovered (SVEIR) epidemic model with demographic turnover, imperfect vaccination, and two transmission routes: direct host-to-host contagion and indirect transmission via contaminated fomites. Indirect transmission is described through an environmental pathogen concentration and a Holling-type dose--response function, accounting for nonlinear incidence at high contamination levels. Threshold conditions separating disease elimination from long-term persistence are expressed in terms of the control reproduction number $\mathcal R_c$, and the classical threshold condition $\mathcal R_c<1$ is derived for the local asymptotic stability of the disease-free equilibrium. For the Holling type~II case, we further obtain an explicit closed-form sufficient condition for the global asymptotic stability of the disease-free equilibrium by applying the Kamgang--Sallet approach for monotone systems with a Metzler infected subsystem. In the absence of vaccination, this criterion recovers the sharp threshold $\mathcal R_0\le 1$ for the global asymptotic stability of the disease-free equilibrium, where $\mathcal R_0$ denotes the basic reproduction number. Conversely, when $\mathcal R_c>1$, we establish uniform persistence of the infection and the existence of at least one endemic equilibrium using persistence theory for semiflows and an acyclicity analysis of the boundary dynamics. Overall, our results quantify the combined impact of vaccination and saturating fomite-mediated transmission on the global behaviour of the model.
